newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-C&W H1 underlying profits to rise.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-C&W H1 underlying profits to rise.

text.p: An expected six percent rise in Cable and Wireless' underlying half-year pretax profits on Wednesday will be masked by a 60 million stg exceptional profit this time and a 200 million stg credit in 1995, analysts say.
C&W, Britain's second biggest telecoms company, is forecast to lift half-year pretax profits before exceptionals to 650-668 million stg on Wednesday, compared to 116 million last time.

After exceptionals, pretax profits are forecast to fall about 12 percent to some 720 million stg against 815 million last time. Analysts have pencilled in a half-year dividend of 3.37-3.40p against 3.08 pence in the first half of 1995.

C&W's profits this half year will be boosted by the disposal of its Asiasat unit, whereas in 1995, half year pretax profits were boosted by the one-off profits of the sale of its stake in Mannesmann Mobilfunk, the German telecoms operator.

It will be new American chief executive Dick Brown's first chance to tell the market what he believes in. Analysts expect him to focus on setting financial preformance targets in terms of costs and revenues.

ABN AMRO Hoare Govett is expecting strong progress of C&W's UK Mercury unit as the group rolls out its networks. Mercury One 2 One, its digital mobile unit jointly owned by U.S. West, is expected to report a 50 million stg loss. Vebakom, C&W's German alliance with Veba and the new addition of RWE, is expected to add a 35 million stg loss.

Most of C&W's profits come from Hong Kong, where it holds a lucrative 57.5 percent stake in Hong Kong Telecommunications. Hong Kong Telecom has already reported steady results broadly in line with expectations.
C&W is denying rampant speculation that it is set to reduce its Hong Kong Telecom stake to below 50 percent in return for better access to the Chinese telecoms market.
Rumours have also swept the market that it is in talks on international cooperation with Sprint, France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom.
Officially, the company has declined to comment on the rumours in newspaper reports and the market, noting only that in the telecoms business, people tend to speak to each other.
Brown's nationality is expected to have played a part in the company's link-up with units of NYNEX and Bell Canada International to create Britain's largest cable operator.
Some analysts expect closer co-operation between C&W and NYNEX, partly in answer to British Telecommunications planned merger with America's MCI to form one of the world's biggest telecoms groups.
